title: Independence
intro: Two events are independent when learning one tells you nothing about the other. For more than two events the definition needs care: every pair can be independent while the whole collection is not.

blocks.caption: The definition of independence of A and B; equivalently P(A | B) = P(A) when P(B) > 0.

blocks.text: The product form is preferred because it is symmetric and makes sense even when $P(B) = 0$. If $A$ and $B$ are independent, so are $A$ and $B^c$, $A^c$ and $B$, and $A^c$ and $B^c$. Independence is not disjointness: two disjoint events with positive probabilities are as dependent as possible, since one excludes the other.

Events $A_1, \dots, A_n$ are (mutually) independent if the product rule holds for every subcollection: $P(A_{i_1}\cdots A_{i_k}) = P(A_{i_1})\cdots P(A_{i_k})$ for all choices of distinct indices. Checking only pairs is not enough, as the sample below shows with two coins and the event that they differ.

items: Products of probabilities: the chance that $n$ independent trials all fail is $(1-p)^n$, so at least one success has probability $1 - (1-p)^n$.
Independent trials are the setting of the binomial, geometric and Poisson distributions (Distributions (#/probability/distributions)) and of every limit theorem.

Modelling: independence is usually an assumption, not a fact. Correlated failures (shared power supplies, common causes) break it and can make rare joint events far more likely than the product suggests.

blocks.text: $A$ and $B$ are conditionally independent given $C$ if $P(AB\mid C) = P(A\mid C)P(B\mid C)$. Neither kind of independence implies the other. Two tosses of a coin of unknown bias are independent given the bias but dependent unconditionally, since the first toss tells you about the bias; this is the structure of Bayesian Inference (#/probability/inference/bayesian-inference).

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from itertools import product
# Two fair coins and their XOR: every pair is independent, the three together are not.
omega = list(product([0, 1], repeat=2))
events = {"A: coin 1 heads": lambda w: w[0] == 1, "B: coin 2 heads": lambda w: w[1] == 1,
          "C: coins differ": lambda w: w[0] != w[1]}
P = lambda f: sum(1 for w in omega if f(w)) / 4
names = list(events)
for i in range(3):
    for j in range(i + 1, 3):
        a, b = events[names[i]], events[names[j]]
        print(f"P({names[i][0]}{names[j][0]}) = {P(lambda w: a(w) and b(w)):.2f}, P({names[i][0]})P({names[j][0]}) = {P(a) * P(b):.2f}")
abc = P(lambda w: all(f(w) for f in events.values()))
print(f"P(ABC) = {abc:.2f} but P(A)P(B)P(C) = {P(events[names[0]]) * P(events[names[1]]) * P(events[names[2]]):.3f}")

blocks.text: Output of the run: for the events A (coin 1 heads), B (coin 2 heads) and C (the coins differ), every pair satisfies $P(\text{pair}) = 0.25 = $ the product. Yet $P(ABC) = 0$, because if both coins are heads they cannot differ, while the product $P(A)P(B)P(C) = 0.125$. Pairwise independent, not mutually independent.

blocks.title: At least one success
blocks.text: A rare event has probability 0.01 per independent trial. What is the probability it happens at least once in 100 trials? How many trials make it 95% likely?

blocks.title: Disjoint and independent?
blocks.text: Can two disjoint events both of positive probability be independent?
solution: Disjoint means $P(A\cap B) = 0$, while independence needs $P(A\cap B) = P(A)P(B) > 0$. So no: disjoint events with positive probability are always dependent.

blocks.title: Independent given the bias
blocks.text: A coin is chosen at random: fair, or with heads probability 0.9. It is tossed twice. Are the two tosses independent?
solution: Given the coin they are independent; unconditionally, a head on the first toss makes the biased coin more likely and so a second head more likely.
